sections.html:
Between Louisville and Frankfort lies Shelby County, a member of the Louisville metro area. Shelbyville is the seat, joined by the incorporated cities of Simpsonville and Pleasureville. Bagdad, Finchville, Christianburg and Clay Village are unincorporated, so only county government serves them.

The county counted 51,243 people in July 2025, compared with 48,113 in April 2020, and has 20,391 housing units. Owners occupy most homes, and the drive to Louisville shapes who buys. Interstate 64 is the main route, with U.S. 60, U.S. 421, KY 53 and KY 55 connecting to it.

With nearly three quarters of homes owned, most sales here involve a long-time resident rather than a landlord.

If your house sits in Shelbyville or Simpsonville, remember that city and county governments each have a say in what the final bill looks like. Ask the PVA which taxing districts apply to your parcel, so the number you see on the bill holds no surprises when you compare it with a buyer's estimate.

sections.h2: What the market looks like for sellers
sections.html:
Shelby County homes carry a median value of $304,800, and the $82,604 median household income supports that level. Buyers are often commuters who work in Louisville and want more space and a quieter street. Houses near Interstate 64 and on the Shelbyville side tend to draw the most attention, while the smaller unincorporated communities appeal to buyers who want acreage.

An owner who needs to move fast has a few choices. A traditional listing can bring the highest price but adds showings, an inspection and a commission. A cash sale gives up some price in exchange for speed and fewer steps. Ask each buyer what they expect from you at closing before you decide, and compare the net you would actually keep.

sections.h2: How the PVA values your home
sections.html:
The Property Valuation Administrator runs a state office at the county level. Every parcel gets a value equal to what a willing buyer and a willing seller would settle on, measured on January 1. Rate setting and payment collection are handled elsewhere, not by the PVA. Your bill combines that assessed value with rates set by state, county and city governments, school boards and special districts. You can reach the PVA at 502-633-4403.

Ownership for tax purposes is fixed on January 1 too. A parcel bought after that date still produces a bill in the former owner's name until the next year, although the PVA tries to mail it to the new owner using the recorded deed. A new owner who gets nothing should call the Sheriff. Sellers should also check that no old bill sits unpaid in their own name.

If you plan to dispute the value, call early. Waiting until the roll closes leaves no room to gather sales data, and the PVA staff can tell you which records matter for your parcel.

One statewide schedule governs (KRS 134.015). Settle the whole bill by November 1 and you save 2 percent. After that, the face amount is due through December 31 with no penalty. Wait until January and 5 percent is added, and later still it becomes 10 percent.

The Sheriff collects the bills, and the office number is 502-633-4324. After April 15, penalties and interest keep building because unpaid claims are filed with the County Clerk, who keeps the delinquent tax records. A statutory collection fee is added to delinquent bills (KRS 134.119). The Sheriff's website has a Current Tax Bill Lookup. Anyone paying someone else's bill, such as a tenant, a lender or a person holding an interest in the property, may do so under KRS 134.119 and can ask to be treated as a transferee.

Start with the PVA. Under KRS 133.045 the assessment roll is open to the public for 13 days starting in early May, six days a week including one Saturday. You have to request a conference with the PVA before any formal appeal. The window repeats each spring.

Bring evidence. Sales of comparable houses nearby, a recent appraisal or repair estimates carry weight, and a request without paperwork rarely moves the number. If the conference leaves you unsatisfied, the notice explains how to file with the local assessment appeals board, and a state level tax appeals board hears cases beyond that.

Homeowners find most of their relief in the Homestead and Disability Exemptions, since the state constitution taxes everything it does not specifically exempt. Nothing applies automatically. The PVA has to receive your application first. Call 502-633-4403 for the current exemption amount and eligibility rules, because they can change from year to year.

sections.h2: Property tax when a Shelby County house sells
sections.html:
At closing the year's tax is usually divided between buyer and seller, and any balance still owing is paid off from the sale. Check the Sheriff's website before you sign, in case an earlier year is still open. The County Clerk handles deed recording and collects the seller's deed tax of $0.50 per $500 block (KRS 142.050).

  • PVA: assessments and exemptions, 502-633-4403.
  • Sheriff, 501 Main Street, Shelbyville: collects tax bills, 502-633-4324.
  • County Clerk: deed recording and delinquent tax records. Check the county website for the number.

Gather a few things before the closing date: the latest tax bill, any exemption paperwork, and a payoff letter if there is a mortgage. The title company or closing attorney will ask for each. A seller who has these ready rarely hits a delay over taxes.

Owing back taxes does not block a sale. Whether you list, sell on your own or take a cash offer, the balance is paid at the closing table. The first step in every case is a current payoff figure from the Sheriff. A cash buyer can usually price in the amount owed and skip the lender's repair and appraisal steps.

Plan the order of things. First, pull the bill on the Sheriff's website or call 502-633-4324 and ask what is owed to date, including any penalty. Second, confirm with the PVA that any exemption you claim is on file. Third, bring the payoff figure to whoever handles the closing so it comes out of your proceeds. The Sheriff's office at 501 Main Street serves walk-ins on weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30, holidays excepted, so a quick visit can settle questions in person.

If the bill is more than one year behind, the claim may already be with the County Clerk. Ask the Clerk for the delinquent record so no year is missed. Those older years add penalties and fees, so clearing them early keeps the closing on schedule.

One more habit helps: write down every call you make and the name of the office, the date and the figure you were given. If a figure changes between your first call and the closing, that record lets you ask why. Keep the written payoff in the closing folder so the person preparing the settlement statement uses the same number you do.

faqs.q: When are Shelby County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Pay the whole bill by November 1 and it drops 2 percent. The printed amount stands through December 31. A January payment costs 5 percent more, anything later costs 10 percent more, and penalties and interest keep building after April 15.

faqs.q: Who gets the bill if a Shelby County house changes hands mid-year?
faqs.a: The bill is mailed to whoever owned the property on January 1. If you bought after that and nothing arrives, phone the Sheriff at 502-633-4324 or search the online bill lookup.

faqs.q: Where can I check a Shelby County tax bill?
faqs.a: Open the Current Tax Bill Lookup on the Sheriff's website or phone the office. Walk-ins are welcome at 501 Main Street in Shelbyville on weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30, except holidays.

faqs.q: What does it take to claim a homestead exemption in Shelby County?
faqs.a: File a formal application with the Property Valuation Administrator, because nothing is granted without one. To hear the present age or disability rules, call 502-633-4403.

faqs.q: What deed tax does a Shelby County seller owe?
faqs.a: Fifty cents on each $500 of price, counting a partial block as a full one. The County Clerk takes the money at recording.
